cards.name: Hydrogen
cards.text: Fuses into helium to power stars. The lightest element, found in every water molecule.

cards.name: Helium
cards.text: Inert and lighter than air: lifts balloons and cools MRI magnets. Never forms compounds.

cards.name: Lithium
cards.text: Lightest metal. Its ions shuttle in phone and EV batteries. Floats and fizzes in water.

cards.name: Beryllium
cards.text: Light and extremely stiff, so it shapes mirrors on space telescopes. Its dust is toxic.

cards.name: Boron
cards.text: Makes Pyrex glass resist heat shock. Also in detergents and reactor control rods.

cards.name: Carbon
cards.text: Bonds in endless chains: the backbone of life, fuels, diamond, and graphite.

cards.name: Nitrogen
cards.text: Makes up 78% of the air. Fixed into fertilizer; liquid N₂ freezes things at −196 °C.

cards.name: Oxygen
cards.text: Fuels combustion and cell respiration. About 21% of the air and 65% of your body mass.

cards.name: Fluorine
cards.text: Most electronegative element. Fluoride in toothpaste hardens enamel; makes non-stick Teflon.

cards.name: Neon
cards.text: Glows red-orange when electrified, lighting up signs. A noble gas that never reacts.

cards.name: Sodium
cards.text: Explodes in water. Bonds with chlorine to make table salt and keeps nerves firing.

cards.name: Magnesium
cards.text: Burns with a blinding white flame (flares, fireworks). Heart of chlorophyll in leaves.

cards.name: Aluminum
cards.text: Light, strong, and rust-resistant: soda cans, aircraft, and foil.

cards.name: Silicon
cards.text: A semiconductor: the brain of computer chips and solar panels. Sand and glass too.

cards.name: Phosphorus
cards.text: Builds DNA and ATP energy molecules. Also in fertilizers and matches.

cards.name: Sulfur
cards.text: Yellow crystals near volcanoes. Used to make sulfuric acid and to harden rubber.

cards.name: Chlorine
cards.text: Kills germs in pools and drinking water. Half of table salt as the Cl⁻ ion.

cards.name: Argon
cards.text: Fills light bulbs and welding shields so hot metal cannot burn. 1% of the air.

cards.name: Potassium
cards.text: Keeps nerves and muscles working (bananas!). Bursts into lilac flame in water.

cards.name: Calcium
cards.text: Builds bones, teeth, and shells. Found in limestone, chalk, and milk.

cards.name: Scandium
cards.text: Strengthens aluminum for bicycle frames, baseball bats, and fighter jets.

cards.name: Titanium
cards.text: As strong as steel but 45% lighter. Used in jets, hip implants, and bike frames.

cards.name: Vanadium
cards.text: Adds strength to steel for wrenches and springs. Its ions come in bright colors.

cards.name: Chromium
cards.text: Chrome plating resists rust and shines. Chromium makes stainless steel stainless.

cards.name: Manganese
cards.text: Makes steel tough enough for railroad tracks and safes. Also in alkaline batteries.

cards.name: Iron
cards.text: Carries O₂ in your blood and makes steel for bridges. Rusts when it meets O₂ and water.

cards.name: Cobalt
cards.text: Gives glass and pottery a deep blue. Used in rechargeable batteries and magnets.

cards.name: Nickel
cards.text: Resists corrosion: coins, stainless steel, and rechargeable batteries. Magnetic.

cards.name: Copper
cards.text: Superb electrical conductor: wires and pipes. Turns green, like the Statue of Liberty.

cards.name: Zinc
cards.text: Coats steel to stop rust (galvanizing). Your body needs it for healing and defense.

cards.name: Gallium
cards.text: A solid that melts at 29.8 °C, so it liquefies in your hand. Used in LEDs and chips.

cards.name: Germanium
cards.text: Semiconductor in the first transistors, fiber optics, and infrared camera lenses.

cards.name: Arsenic
cards.text: A famous poison. In tiny amounts it makes semiconductors for LEDs and solar cells.

cards.name: Selenium
cards.text: Conducts better in light: solar cells and old photocopiers. Needed in tiny amounts.

cards.name: Bromine
cards.text: One of two elements that are liquid at room temperature. Red-brown, smelly fumes.

cards.name: Krypton
cards.text: Noble gas in high-speed camera flashes and bright lamps. Once helped define the meter.

cards.name: Rubidium
cards.text: Its vapor keeps time in atomic clocks. Soft metal that reacts violently with water.

cards.name: Strontium
cards.text: Burns bright red in fireworks and flares. Its ion mimics calcium in bones.

cards.name: Yttrium
cards.text: Gives old TV screens and LEDs their red and white glow. Also coats jet engines.

cards.name: Zirconium
cards.text: Barely absorbs neutrons, so it wraps nuclear fuel rods. Cubic zirconia is its oxide.

cards.name: Niobium
cards.text: Makes superconducting magnets for MRI machines and strong, light steel alloys.

cards.name: Molybdenum
cards.text: Keeps steel strong at extreme heat. Plants need it to fix nitrogen.

cards.name: Technetium
cards.text: First man-made element. Tc-99m is injected to image organs. All isotopes are radioactive.

cards.name: Ruthenium
cards.text: Hardens platinum and palladium, and coats electrical contacts so they last.

cards.name: Rhodium
cards.text: Rare metal in catalytic converters that turn exhaust gases into safer ones.

cards.name: Palladium
cards.text: Soaks up hydrogen like a sponge. Also in catalytic converters and electronics.

cards.name: Silver
cards.text: Conducts electricity and heat better than any metal. Tarnishes black as Ag₂S.

cards.name: Cadmium
cards.text: Used in old NiCd batteries and yellow paint. Toxic, so now mostly phased out.

cards.name: Indium
cards.text: Indium tin oxide makes phone touch screens clear and conductive.

cards.name: Tin
cards.text: Coats steel food cans. Mixed with copper it makes bronze, and with lead, solder.

cards.name: Antimony
cards.text: Added to plastics and fabrics as a flame retardant, and to lead to harden it.

cards.name: Tellurium
cards.text: Used in thin-film solar panels and rewritable discs. Makes breath smell like garlic.

cards.name: Iodine
cards.text: Added to table salt (iodized) because the thyroid needs it. Purple vapor when heated.

cards.name: Xenon
cards.text: Heavy noble gas that fuels spacecraft ion engines and bright car headlamps.

cards.name: Cesium
cards.text: Vibrations of Cs-133 atoms define the second. Explodes in water.

cards.name: Barium
cards.text: Burns apple-green in fireworks. Barium sulfate drinks make the gut show on X-rays.

cards.name: Lanthanum
cards.text: Sharpens camera lenses and boosts hybrid-car batteries. Namesake of the lanthanides.

cards.name: Cerium
cards.text: Makes the sparks in lighter flints and polishes glass. Most abundant rare earth.

cards.name: Praseodymium
cards.text: Tints glass and ceramics yellow-green, and strengthens magnets and welding goggles.

cards.name: Neodymium
cards.text: Neodymium magnets are the strongest everyday magnets: headphones, motors, hard drives.

cards.name: Promethium
cards.text: Radioactive and rare. Once powered glow-in-the-dark dials and long-life batteries.

cards.name: Samarium
cards.text: Makes strong, heat-resistant magnets. Named after the mineral samarskite.

cards.name: Europium
cards.text: Makes the red in old TVs and the glow that protects euro banknotes from forgery.

cards.name: Gadolinium
cards.text: Its compounds brighten MRI scans. Also an excellent neutron absorber.

cards.name: Terbium
cards.text: Makes green phosphors for lamps and screens, and is used in sonar devices.

cards.name: Dysprosium
cards.text: Helps magnets stay magnetic at high heat, as in electric car motors.

cards.name: Holmium
cards.text: Has the strongest magnetic moment of any element. Used in lasers and magnets.

cards.name: Erbium
cards.text: Boosts light signals in fiber-optic cables and tints glass pink.

cards.name: Thulium
cards.text: One of the rarest lanthanides. Used in lasers and portable X-ray units.

cards.name: Ytterbium
cards.text: Used in some of the most precise atomic clocks, and in lasers.

cards.name: Lutetium
cards.text: Used in crystals for PET scanners. The densest and hardest lanthanide.

cards.name: Hafnium
cards.text: Insulates modern computer chips, and shields reactors by absorbing neutrons.

cards.name: Tantalum
cards.text: Tiny capacitors in phones and laptops. So corrosion-resistant it is used in implants.

cards.name: Tungsten
cards.text: Melts at 3422 °C, highest of any metal. Glowed in old light-bulb filaments.

cards.name: Rhenium
cards.text: Rare metal alloyed into jet-engine blades that must survive extreme heat.

cards.name: Osmium
cards.text: The densest naturally occurring element. Used in pen tips and electrical contacts.

cards.name: Iridium
cards.text: A layer rich in iridium marks the asteroid impact that ended the dinosaurs.

cards.name: Platinum
cards.text: Resists corrosion and speeds reactions: catalytic converters, jewelry, lab equipment.

cards.name: Gold
cards.text: Almost never reacts, so it never tarnishes. Used in jewelry, coins, and electronics.

cards.name: Mercury
cards.text: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature. Toxic; once used in thermometers.

cards.name: Thallium
cards.text: Soft metal with very toxic compounds. Used in some infrared optics and sensors.

cards.name: Lead
cards.text: Dense and soft: shields X-rays and was used in pipes and paint. Toxic to nerves.

cards.name: Bismuth
cards.text: Grows rainbow-colored stair-step crystals. Barely radioactive for such a heavy element.

cards.name: Polonium
cards.text: Discovered by Marie Curie and named for her homeland, Poland. Intensely radioactive.

cards.name: Astatine
cards.text: Least abundant natural element: under a gram exists in Earth’s crust at once.

cards.name: Radon
cards.text: Radioactive gas that seeps from soil into basements. Test kits check homes for it.

cards.name: Francium
cards.text: Extremely rare and radioactive. Its longest-lived isotope lasts only 22 minutes.

cards.name: Radium
cards.text: Discovered by the Curies. Once painted on watch dials; intensely radioactive.

cards.name: Actinium
cards.text: Glows pale blue in the dark from its radioactivity. Namesake of the actinides.

cards.name: Thorium
cards.text: More abundant than uranium and a candidate nuclear fuel. Once in lantern mantles.

cards.name: Protactinium
cards.text: Rare radioactive element found in uranium ore. Decays into actinium.

cards.name: Uranium
cards.text: U-235 splits to release huge energy in nuclear power plants. Very dense.

cards.name: Neptunium
cards.text: First transuranium element, made in 1940. Traces form in uranium ore and reactors.

cards.name: Plutonium
cards.text: Pu-238 gives off heat that powers deep-space probes such as Voyager.

cards.name: Americium
cards.text: A tiny bit of Am-241 ionizes the air inside a smoke detector to sense fires.

cards.name: Curium
cards.text: Named for Marie and Pierre Curie. Used in the X-ray tools on Mars rovers.

cards.name: Berkelium
cards.text: Named for Berkeley, California, where it was first made. Used to build heavier elements.

cards.name: Californium
cards.text: Strong neutron emitter used to start nuclear reactors and to find oil and metals.

cards.name: Einsteinium
cards.text: First found in debris from a 1952 hydrogen bomb test. Named for Albert Einstein.

cards.name: Fermium
cards.text: Made in nuclear reactors and test debris. Named for physicist Enrico Fermi.

cards.name: Mendelevium
cards.text: Named for Mendeleev, who built the first periodic table. Made a few atoms at a time.

cards.name: Nobelium
cards.text: Named for Alfred Nobel. Only a few atoms are made at once and decay in minutes.

cards.name: Lawrencium
cards.text: Named for cyclotron inventor Ernest Lawrence. The last of the actinides.

cards.name: Rutherfordium
cards.text: Honors Ernest Rutherford, who found the atom’s nucleus. Made only in labs.

cards.name: Dubnium
cards.text: Named for Dubna, Russia, where it was made. Lasts seconds to hours.

cards.name: Seaborgium
cards.text: Named while Glenn Seaborg was alive, the first element to honor a living person.

cards.name: Bohrium
cards.text: Named for Niels Bohr, who explained electron energy levels in atoms.

cards.name: Hassium
cards.text: Named for Hesse, Germany. Expected to be a dense metal like osmium.

cards.name: Meitnerium
cards.text: Honors Lise Meitner, who helped explain nuclear fission. Predicted configuration.

cards.name: Darmstadtium
cards.text: Named for Darmstadt, Germany. Only a few atoms ever seen. Predicted configuration.

cards.name: Roentgenium
cards.text: Honors Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays. Short-lived; predicted configuration.

cards.name: Copernicium
cards.text: Honors Nicolaus Copernicus. May be a gas or liquid, like mercury’s heavy cousin.

cards.name: Nihonium
cards.text: First element discovered in Asia, named for Japan (Nihon). Lasts only seconds.

cards.name: Flerovium
cards.text: Named for the Flerov Lab in Russia. May act like a noble gas. Lasts seconds.

cards.name: Moscovium
cards.text: Named for the Moscow region. A few atoms made; each decays in under a second.

cards.name: Livermorium
cards.text: Named for Lawrence Livermore Lab. A few atoms last only milliseconds.

cards.name: Tennessine
cards.text: Named for Tennessee. Made by smashing calcium into berkelium. Short-lived.

cards.name: Oganesson
cards.text: The heaviest known element, named for Yuri Oganessian. Only a few atoms made.

cards.name: Hydrogen Ion
cards.text: A bare proton in water. More H⁺ ions means a lower pH and a stronger acid.

cards.name: Lithium Ion
cards.text: Li⁺ ions swim between the electrodes of a rechargeable battery as it charges and discharges.

cards.name: Sodium Ion
cards.text: Na⁺ rushing through nerve membranes carries signals. Isoelectronic with neon.

cards.name: Potassium Ion
cards.text: K⁺ keeps your heartbeat steady and nerves firing. Plants take it up from fertilizer.

cards.name: Silver Ion
cards.text: Kills bacteria, so it is used in wound dressings and water filters. Darkens in light.

cards.name: Copper(I) Ion
cards.text: Forms red-orange copper(I) oxide. Its full 3d¹⁰ shell makes it stable.

cards.name: Magnesium Ion
cards.text: Sits at the center of every chlorophyll molecule. Epsom salt is MgSO₄.

cards.name: Calcium Ion
cards.text: Hardens bones, teeth, and shells, and triggers muscle contraction. Causes hard water.

cards.name: Strontium Ion
cards.text: Acts like calcium and lodges in bones. That is why Sr-90 from fallout is dangerous.

cards.name: Barium Ion
cards.text: Insoluble BaSO₄ shows the gut on X-rays. Soluble barium compounds are poisonous.

cards.name: Zinc Ion
cards.text: Helps hundreds of enzymes work and heals wounds. Zinc oxide is in sunscreen.

cards.name: Iron(II) Ion
cards.text: Fe²⁺ in hemoglobin grabs O₂ in your lungs. 4s electrons leave before 3d ones.

cards.name: Copper(II) Ion
cards.text: Colors copper(II) sulfate crystals and solutions a bright blue.

cards.name: Nickel(II) Ion
cards.text: Gives solutions a green color. Nickel plating protects metal and makes it shine.

cards.name: Manganese(II) Ion
cards.text: Faint pink in solution. A half-filled 3d⁵ shell makes it a stable ion.

cards.name: Lead(II) Ion
cards.text: In old paint and pipes. Lead ions harm the nervous system, especially in children.

cards.name: Tin(II) Ion
cards.text: Stannous fluoride in toothpaste. Tin(II) ions are also a mild reducing agent.

cards.name: Aluminum Ion
cards.text: Alum’s Al³⁺ clumps dirt so plants can filter it. Rubies and sapphires are Al₂O₃.

cards.name: Iron(III) Ion
cards.text: Fe³⁺ is the ion in rust (Fe₂O₃). Its half-filled 3d⁵ shell is extra stable.

cards.name: Chromium(III) Ion
cards.text: Makes rubies red and emeralds green. Used to tan leather and in green pigments.

cards.name: Nitride Ion
cards.text: Forms nitrides like Li₃N and Mg₃N₂. Gains 3 e⁻ to match neon.

cards.name: Oxide Ion
cards.text: Forms oxides such as rust (Fe₂O₃) and quicklime (CaO). Gains 2 e⁻ to match neon.

cards.name: Fluoride Ion
cards.text: Fluoride in toothpaste and tap water hardens tooth enamel. Gains 1 e⁻ to match neon.

cards.name: Phosphide Ion
cards.text: Forms phosphides like Zn₃P₂, used to poison rodents. Gains 3 e⁻ to match argon.

cards.name: Sulfide Ion
cards.text: Forms sulfides, like the black tarnish on silver (Ag₂S). Gains 2 e⁻ to match argon.

cards.name: Chloride Ion
cards.text: Pairs with Na⁺ to make table salt, and fills your stomach acid as HCl. Matches argon.

cards.name: Bromide Ion
cards.text: AgBr crystals in photographic film darken in light. Gains 1 e⁻ to match krypton.

cards.name: Iodide Ion
cards.text: Iodide in iodized salt keeps the thyroid supplied. Gains 1 e⁻ to match xenon.

cards.name: Ammonium Ion
cards.text: Ammonium nitrate and sulfate feed crops. Forms when NH₃ picks up an H⁺.

cards.name: Hydronium Ion
cards.text: What H⁺ really looks like in water. Its concentration sets the pH.

cards.name: Hydroxide Ion
cards.text: Makes solutions basic. NaOH and milk of magnesia release it.

cards.name: Nitrate Ion
cards.text: Plants absorb it as food, but fertilizer runoff pollutes lakes and wells.

cards.name: Nitrite Ion
cards.text: Sodium nitrite preserves bacon and ham and keeps cured meat pink.

cards.name: Sulfate Ion
cards.text: In Epsom salt, gypsum, and car-battery acid (H₂SO₄).

cards.name: Sulfite Ion
cards.text: Sulfites keep dried fruit and wine from spoiling.

cards.name: Carbonate Ion
cards.text: In limestone, chalk, marble, and seashells. Fizzes in acid, releasing CO₂.

cards.name: Bicarbonate Ion
cards.text: Baking soda and your blood use it to keep pH steady. The shape is trigonal planar around its carbon.

cards.name: Phosphate Ion
cards.text: In DNA, bones, ATP, and fertilizer. Phosphates also fuel algae blooms.

cards.name: Acetate Ion
cards.text: Acetate comes from acetic acid, the sour part of vinegar. The shape is trigonal planar around the carbon of its COO⁻ group.

cards.name: Permanganate Ion
cards.text: Gives solutions a deep purple color and is a strong oxidizer.

cards.name: Hydrogen-1
cards.text: Protium: one proton, no neutron. Over 99.98% of all hydrogen, and the Sun’s fusion fuel.

cards.name: Hydrogen-2
cards.text: Deuterium: 0.015% of hydrogen. D₂O “heavy water” slows neutrons in some nuclear reactors.

cards.name: Hydrogen-3
cards.text: Tritium: radioactive, half-life 12.3 years. Powers glow-in-the-dark exit signs and watch dials.

cards.name: Helium-4
cards.text: Over 99.99% of helium. An alpha particle is a He-4 nucleus shot out by radioactive decay.

cards.name: Lithium-6
cards.text: The rarer lithium (7.6%). Absorbs neutrons to make tritium for fusion research.

cards.name: Lithium-7
cards.text: 92.4% of lithium, so the average mass 6.94 sits close to 7.

cards.name: Boron-10
cards.text: 19.9% of boron. Absorbs neutrons strongly: used in reactor control rods and shielding.

cards.name: Boron-11
cards.text: 80.1% of boron. Pulls the average mass to 10.81, much closer to 11 than to 10.

cards.name: Carbon-12
cards.text: 98.9% of carbon. By definition, exactly 12 atomic mass units.

cards.name: Carbon-13
cards.text: Stable and 1.1% of carbon. Scientists trace it through food webs and metabolism.

cards.name: Carbon-14
cards.text: Half-life 5,730 years. Dates fossils and artifacts by measuring how much C-14 is left.

cards.name: Oxygen-16
cards.text: 99.76% of oxygen, the one you breathe. 8 protons plus 8 neutrons.

cards.name: Oxygen-18
cards.text: Heavier oxygen. Ratios of O-18 in ice cores reveal past temperatures.

cards.name: Chlorine-35
cards.text: About 76% of all chlorine. Mixed with Cl-37, it makes the average mass 35.45.

cards.name: Chlorine-37
cards.text: About 24% of all chlorine. Two extra neutrons pull the average above 35.

cards.name: Potassium-40
cards.text: Half-life 1.25 billion years. Tiny amounts in bananas, your body, and rocks that date.

cards.name: Cobalt-60
cards.text: Gamma emitter, half-life 5.3 years. Used in cancer radiotherapy and food irradiation.

cards.name: Strontium-90
cards.text: Fission product, half-life 29 years. Mimics calcium and collects in bones.

cards.name: Iodine-131
cards.text: Radioactive iodine, half-life 8 days. Doctors use it to image and treat the thyroid.

cards.name: Cesium-137
cards.text: Fission product with a 30-year half-life. Used in medical and industrial gauges.

cards.name: Radon-222
cards.text: Radioactive gas, half-life 3.8 days, seeping from soil into basements. Test your home.

cards.name: Radium-226
cards.text: Half-life 1,600 years. Once painted on watch dials; the Curies discovered radium.

cards.name: Uranium-235
cards.text: Splits when hit by a neutron and releases huge energy. Fuel for nuclear power plants.

cards.name: Uranium-238
cards.text: 99.3% of uranium. Half-life 4.5 billion years; used to date Earth’s oldest rocks.

cards.name: Americium-241
cards.text: Half-life 432 years. Its alpha particles keep smoke detectors on watch.
